assign.now: Jobs 1 and 3 done. Self-agreement is WORSE than Sonnet-vs-baseline -- the rubric is the bottleneck, not the model.

log.msg: **DELIVERABLE 1 -- REPEATABILITY, and it is the headline of this task. The baseline does not reproduce itself.** Same model (claude-opus-5[1m]), same rubric text, same 18 byte-identical PNGs, independent context, scores written before reading pass A. n=18. | dim | rawMAE | drift | centMAE | sdA | sdB | max abs d | Spearman | ICC(2,1) | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | layout | 6.44 | -3.78 | 5.60 | 8.37 | 8.46 | 20 | +0.361 | 0.600 | | typography | 8.22 | -6.44 | 5.95 | 5.91 | 7.02 | 14 | +0.473 | 0.285 | | contrast | 5.33 | -3.00 | 5.22 | 10.74 | 7.50 | 16 | **+0.793** | 0.728 | | density | 4.67 | -2.44 | 4.40 | 10.13 | 9.72 | 14 | **+0.780** | 0.822 | | hierarchy | 10.94 | -6.28 | 9.31 | 10.62 | 11.98 | **30** | +0.335 | 0.359 | | **overall** | **7.89** | -5.33 | 5.93 | 8.21 | 8.15 | 16 | **+0.507** | 0.510 | Flat rows 0/18 in both passes; mean within-row span 13.3 (A) and 14.9 (B), so neither pass is a constant generator. Systematic drift: pass B is lower on all six dimensions (-2.4 to -6.4), i.e. the SCALE moved between passes even though the anchors were fixed in writing. Second pass written to rubric-v2/pass-b.json; baseline.json untouched.

**THE CEILING RESULT: Sonnet agrees with the baseline better than the baseline agrees with itself.** Sonnet-vs-passA MAE 6.44 / Spearman +0.625. Baseline-vs-baseline MAE 7.89 / Spearman +0.507. And against my blind pass B, Sonnet scores **MAE 4.44 / Spearman +0.689** -- its best agreement with anything measured in this program. So no tier can be ranked against this baseline: the measuring stick has wider error bars than the differences it is being used to detect. The vision-baseline task listed this as caveat (c) -- unmeasured self-consistency -- and guessed a second pass would move pages by only a few points. Measured: it moves them 16 points at the top of the list (/notes/git-branch-names/ 78 -> 62, /framework/core/Page/ 71 -> 56, /framework/ext/layout/ 74 -> 60) and it reorders the corpus.

**MAE-alone is a trap, and here is the version of the trap that bites the BASELINE.** Best-constant control against pass A, per dimension: layout const 67 -> MAE 5.33 | typography const 73 -> 4.78 | contrast const 72 -> 8.72 | density const 67 -> 7.89 | hierarchy const 72 -> 8.00 | overall const 70 -> 5.56. Compare each axis drift-corrected self-MAE to its own constant (ratio below 1 means the axis beats doing nothing): **contrast 0.60, density 0.56 -- real signal. layout 1.05, overall 1.07, hierarchy 1.16, typography 1.25 -- no better than a constant, or worse.** So on four of six axes the strongest available model, re-scoring pixels it has already scored, carries no more information than a fixed number. That is the same hazard the vision-baseline task found in Haiku, found in the source of truth.

**Statistical significance, stated so nobody over-reads the coefficients.** At n=18 critical rho is 0.475 (p=.05) and 0.600 (p=.01). Of the baseline's six self-agreement coefficients only **contrast (+0.793) and density (+0.780) clear p=.01**; overall (+0.507) and typography (+0.473) sit on or under the p=.05 line; layout (+0.361) and hierarchy (+0.335) are inside noise. **The baseline's own ordering of the corpus is not statistically reproducible on four of its five axes.**

**`overall` is not a holistic judgement -- it is the arithmetic mean of the five, in both passes.** The rubric says overall is 'informed by the five but NOT their mean'. Measured: Spearman(mean-of-5, overall) = **0.983** in pass A and **0.982** in pass B, with MAE 0.97 and 1.89. The instruction is inert -- both passes computed the mean while believing they did not. And the mean is the MORE reproducible of the two (mean5 A-vs-B Spearman 0.552 vs judged-overall 0.507), because averaging axes cancels noise a single judgement does not. **Verdict: delete `overall` as a scored axis and derive it.** Free reliability, one less number, and it makes room for the contrast split without exceeding six axes (RULE#18: deleting beats adding).

**WHY the axes fail, and it is one cause not five (RULE#18: suspect the rule).** The two axes that reproduce are the two whose anchors name **locatable pixel facts**, and whose prose in both passes converged on the same named objects: contrast -> 'the control strip is grey on grey', 'the checkerboard runs behind the body copy'; density -> '75% empty checkerboard', '150px of trailing white in the stage'. The four that fail are anchored on **abstractions** -- 'deliberate alignment', 'a type scale with real contrast', 'does the eye have a path' -- and the two passes picked DIFFERENT facts to weigh. Worked example, /web/layout/flow/: pass A charged the illegible 8px rail text to `contrast` and gave typography 66; pass B charged the same pixels to `typography` and gave it 52. Same defect, same image, different axis. The axes are not under-specified about the pages, they are under-specified about **which axis owns which defect** -- plus a genuine scale drift (-2.4 to -6.4 on every axis between passes) that fixed prose anchors did not prevent.

**DELIVERABLE 3 -- THE RESCALE, VERIFIED. The monotone claim is exactly right; the rescale itself should be rejected on other grounds.** (1) **Spearman-cannot-move check PASSES:** delta Spearman = 0.000e+0 and delta Pearson = -1.11e-16 (float noise); the two rank vectors are identical. `70.2 + (s-66.2)*2.04` is strictly increasing so order is preserved by construction -- **no bug, the published +0.625 survives the transform exactly.** (2) Published post-rescale figures reproduce: MAE 6.13 -> computed **6.12**; bias -4.00 -> **+0.02**; sd -> **8.21**. The published 'sd 7.98' is the POPULATION sd of the baseline while the slope 2.04 is the SAMPLE sd ratio (8.21/4.02) -- a convention mismatch in the write-up, not an error in the map. (3) **But the rescale makes MAE worse than doing nothing.** Post-rescale MAE 6.12 vs constant-70 5.56 and constant-72 5.22. Sweeping the slope k: MAE is minimised at **k=0.65 (MAE 4.66)** -- MAE wants Sonnet COMPRESSED FURTHER, not expanded; k=2.04 costs 1.46 MAE to buy honest spread. That is a legitimate trade but it must be stated as one, not as 'fixes it'.

**THE RESCALE CANNOT REACH THE TAIL, AND NO MONOTONE MAP CAN.** The rescale exists to fix Sonnet hedging into 60-72. On the page that matters -- /web/layout/flow/, the worst in the corpus at 44 -- Sonnet says 62, which is joint-lowest with three pages the baseline puts at 64, 68 and 71. A monotone map returns one output per input, so **those four pages must receive the same score**; the best any monotone map can do leaves flow at least **17.8 points high**. After the published rescale flow reads **61.6, still 17.6 high**. An L1-optimal step function over Sonnet's overall bottoms out at MAE 3.00 in-sample and is **not even monotone** (60->68, 62->53.5, 63->72), which is itself proof the ordering is too weak to calibrate against. **A scorer that cannot say 'this page is a 44' cannot flag a bad page, which is the only thing the metric is for.** Rescaling relabels the hedge; it does not remove it.

**The rescale is also an in-sample fit, and the second baseline pass shows the overfit.** Its two parameters (70.2, 2.04) are the baseline's own mean and sd -- unavailable for 168 unscored pages, so the transform is not applicable in production without first hand-scoring a calibration set. Tested against my independent pass B: **Sonnet RAW gets MAE 4.44, Sonnet RESCALED gets 6.61.** The rescale improves agreement with the pass it was fitted to and degrades agreement with the pass it was not. **Recommendation: ship Sonnet raw, publish the spread alongside every score, and do not rescale.**

**REOPENING one vision-baseline verdict (RULE#2, new evidence).** 'taste.json is closer to how pages look' does not replicate on ORDERING. Against pass A taste is Spearman +0.266; against my blind pass B it is **-0.141** -- it changes sign. math likewise goes -0.039 -> -0.067. What DOES survive both passes: (a) math is unusable -- MAE 12.78 / 18.33, bias +11.7, hard floor of 70, Pearson -0.393 vs A; (b) taste's LEVEL is right (bias -1.33) while its ordering is inside noise against either pass; (c) Sonnet is the only scorer whose ordering is significant against BOTH baselines (+0.625 vs A, +0.689 vs B). So the fix list from vision-baseline stands -- the four calibration bugs are real and `width-used` is still the top one -- but 'taste beats math at ranking' was a difference measured inside the baseline's own noise, and only the MAE/bias half of that verdict holds.

assign.now: Job 2: contrast diagnosed and split. Running a 4-pass controlled experiment (Sonnet x2 on v1, x2 on v2) to test whether fact-anchored axes actually reproduce.

log.msg: **DELIVERABLE 2, part 1 -- what `contrast` was conflating, read out of pass A's own prose.** Two jobs, and the prose separates them cleanly. **Job 1, legibility (can you read it):** '/web/nav/sidebar/ -- the bottom control strip is the failure: standard in a grey select, FILL in light grey, FLOW in pale orange... a functional control surface you can barely see' | '/framework/ui/panel/ -- near-invisible grey on grey' | '/web/layout/flow/ -- the escaped rail text is ~8px teal on light grey and cannot be read at all' | '/framework/styles/layers/theme/lew42/ -- the checkerboard transparency ground runs directly behind the body copy'. **Job 2, emphasis (does emphasis mean anything):** '/framework/ext/toc/ -- strong to a fault... the chips are near-black blobs at maximum contrast dropped mid-sentence, so emphasis stops meaning anything' | '/web/layout/flow/ -- scattered mid-sentence words are tinted as if they were links when they are not, so emphasis reads as noise' | '/framework/audit/ -- the strongest emphasis system in the set: orange underlined links read unmistakably as links, dark chips as code, bold as bold' | '/framework/ai/ -- the outlined VISION pill is a nice piece of emphasis'.

**The two jobs CANCEL on the same page, which is the mechanism behind contrast's noise.** /framework/ext/toc/ scored **72**: its legibility is ~90 ('the type is crisp', no weak region anywhere) and its emphasis is ~45 (chips over-applied until they mark nothing). One number averaged a 90 and a 45 and reported 72, which describes neither. Mirror image on the five control-strip pages (sidebar 58, panel 62, tags 62, crumbs 62, children 66): legibility ~40-55 with emphasis ~70-80. **A page can fail legibility while passing emphasis, or the reverse, and v1 forced them into one score.** Splitting is therefore correct on construct grounds -- but see the next line, because the measurement says it was NOT the axis to fix first.

**COURSE CORRECTION on the brief's premise, with the number that forces it (RULE#18: suspect the rule before editing the pages).** The brief targets `contrast` because it has the worst CROSS-MODEL agreement (Sonnet MAE 9.00, per-dim Spearman +0.335). Now that intra-rater agreement exists, that reading inverts: **`contrast` has the BEST self-agreement of the five (Spearman +0.793, ICC 0.728, and the only axis besides density to beat its own constant control).** Cross-model disagreement conflates an under-specified axis with a weaker model failing a well-specified one -- and contrast is the second case. The genuinely under-specified axes, invisible until repeatability was measured, are **hierarchy (self-Spearman +0.335, ICC 0.359, max disagreement 30 points) and typography (ICC 0.285)** -- neither of which the brief questioned, and both of which score WORSE than a constant. So: the split still ships, because the prose proves two constructs and the two are separable at no cost; but it is not the fix, and shipping it alone would have hardened the one axis that already worked while leaving the two broken ones in place.

**Axis count held at six, by deleting rather than adding (RULE#18).** v1 was 5 scored axes + a judged `overall` = 6 numbers. v2 is **layout, typography, legibility, emphasis, density, hierarchy = 6 scored axes, and `overall` is computed as their mean, not judged.** Same six numbers reported, one fewer judgement asked for, and the headline number gets more reliable rather than less (mean-of-axes reproduced at Spearman 0.552 vs judged-overall 0.507). `polish` stays rejected on the original grounds; `emphasis` is not `polish` -- it has its own 30/60/90 anchored on a countable fact (how many emphasis devices, does each carry one meaning, is any applied to over ~15% of its text).

**What v2 changes, and why each change traces to a measured failure.** (1) **Every anchor is a countable or locatable fact**, because the two axes that reproduced are the two whose anchors named objects -- v2 asks for distinct left-edge counts, dead-gutter percentages, longest-line character counts, counts of unreadable regions, counts of emphasis devices, percent-of-viewport-carrying-content, and a count of elements competing for first look. (2) **An attribution table naming which axis owns which defect**, because the measured failure was cross-axis attribution drift, not disagreement about pages: the same 8px rail text went to `contrast` in pass A and `typography` in pass B. (3) **The prose must name the region and give the number** -- a sentence that could have been written without seeing that particular image is rejected. (4) **A flat-row check** ('if all six land within 4 points you have formed one impression and copied it six times'), which is the Haiku failure mode written into the instrument as a guard. Rubric v2 in full: rubric-v2/rubric.md.

**The experiment now running -- and it is the one that decides ready / not-ready.** A rubric rewrite is a hypothesis, so it gets a control rather than an assertion. Four independent claude-sonnet-5 CLI passes, identical harness, identical 18 byte-identical PNGs in identical order, differing ONLY in the rubric file they read: **2 passes on v1 verbatim, 2 passes on v2.** Each is fenced to Read + Write and told explicitly not to open any existing score file, so no pass can see the baseline, pass B, or its sibling. Measuring **test-retest** within each rubric (per-axis centred MAE, sd, flat-row count, Spearman, ICC) gives the first clean answer to the question underneath this whole task: is the noise in the RUBRIC or in the SCORER? v1 test-retest is the control; if v2 does not beat it, the problem is not the wording and 168 pages must wait.

assign.now: Experiment came back NEGATIVE: my fact-anchored v2 is far WORSE than v1. Adding a third pass per arm before writing the verdict.

log.msg: **THE EXPERIMENT RETURNED A NEGATIVE RESULT AND I AM REPORTING IT AS SUCH: rubric v2 -- my rewrite -- is a REGRESSION, and by a wide margin.** claude-sonnet-5 test-retest, two independent passes per arm, identical harness, identical images, only the rubric file differs. | | v1 (control) | v2 (mine) | |---|---|---| | mean-of-axes Spearman | **+0.704** | **+0.039** | | mean-of-axes ICC | **0.723** | 0.041 | | mean-of-axes centred MAE | **3.20** | 7.16 | | centred MAE / best-constant | **0.68** | 1.16 | Per shared axis, v1 -> v2 Spearman: layout **+0.702 -> -0.027**, typography +0.576 -> -0.012, hierarchy **+0.740 -> +0.317**, density +0.655 -> +0.662. **Three of four shared axes collapsed to zero and only density survived.** RULE#18: a fix that satisfies a metric while making the thing worse is a regression. **v2 does not ship.**

**WHY v2 failed, diagnosed from the prose -- and it is a defect I authored, not a bad run.** Both v2 passes wrote careful, fact-citing feedback; neither is degenerate. The bug is that **v2's anchors list four independent criteria per axis and never say how to combine them**, so the score became a function of which criterion the scorer noticed first. Worked example, /notes/git-branch-names/ on `layout`: pass 1 scored **90** -- 'a single left edge at 50px runs consistently through the h1, code block, prose and table, with nothing clipped' (criterion a). Pass 2 scored **35** -- 'the single content column tops out at x=833, leaving a right-hand dead region of ~447px, or 34.9% of the 1280px width' (criterion b). **Both readings are correct, both follow the rubric as written, and they differ by 55 points.** Same failure on /web/nav/sidebar/ layout (30 vs 88). v1's holistic band -- 'competent, undesigned... but something obvious holds it back' -- invites one graded impression that implicitly averages the criteria and lands stably; v2's OR-joined 30/60/90 bands turn a difference in *attention* into a 30-55 point difference in *score*.

**Second v2 defect: discretising a continuous judgement AMPLIFIES noise.** v2 layout sd 24.60 / 18.34 with both passes using the full [30,90] range, against v1 layout sd 9.73 / 11.58. Mean within-row span went from v1's 13.1 / 11.2 to v2's **34.8 / 28.4**. Threshold anchors ('at most 2 distinct left edges', 'a dead region over 35%') create cliffs: a borderline read -- is that three left edges or two? -- flips a band and moves the score 30 points. The instrument got more sensitive and less accurate at the same time. (Memory: 'instruments find themselves first' -- this one found its own defect on the first run, which is the good outcome.)

**The contrast split itself: two constructs confirmed, but splitting did not stabilise them -- it gave the noise two places to go.** legibility-vs-emphasis Spearman across the corpus: **+0.527 in pass 1, -0.300 in pass 2** -- so yes, they are not one construct renamed (a rename would sit near +1.0). Against Opus pass A's `contrast`, legibility correlates +0.398 / +0.389 and emphasis +0.196 / -0.096, i.e. **v1's `contrast` was mostly the legibility half**. But test-retest: legibility Spearman **+0.005** (ICC -0.102), emphasis **+0.386** (ICC 0.135) -- against v1's fused contrast at +0.279. Worked example, /framework/ext/toc/: pass 1 legibility 90 / emphasis 75, pass 2 legibility 60 / emphasis 82 -- the two passes moved in OPPOSITE directions on both halves. **Verdict: the construct analysis is right and the split is premature. Ship it only once the anchors have a single criterion each.**

**AND the vision-baseline headline does not replicate either.** Its result was Sonnet Spearman **+0.625** vs pass A, 'the only statistically significant ordering measured'. Two fresh Sonnet passes on the identical v1 rubric and the identical 18 PNGs score **+0.206 and +0.242** on judged overall (+0.184 and +0.264 on mean-of-axes); averaging the two gives +0.247. Against my blind pass B the same runs give +0.444 and +0.492. **So the same model, same rubric, same pixels yields Spearman anywhere from +0.18 to +0.69 depending on the run and on which baseline pass you measure against.** At n=18 the coefficient's own sampling spread is roughly as wide as the range of values the study was trying to distinguish -- which is why +0.625 read as a decisive result and is not one. Every headline number in this program so far is a single draw.

**A reframe the numbers force: Sonnet is MORE self-consistent than the Opus 'source of truth', and the two are measuring different things.** Sonnet on v1: test-retest ICC **0.723**, Spearman +0.704. Opus on v1: test-retest ICC **0.510**, Spearman +0.507. Sonnet-vs-Opus: ~+0.2. Two scorers can each be reliable and still disagree -- which is what reliable-but-different looks like, and it means **the premise that Opus's pass is the ground truth to be matched is not supported**: it is the less repeatable of the two. Whatever ground truth this program needs has to come from something more stable than one pass by one model -- an averaged panel, or Mike.

**Cost, measured, as production numbers (deliverable input).** claude-sonnet-5, one pass over 18 images, this harness: **$0.98 / $1.28 / $1.53 / $2.54 per 18-image pass = $0.055 / $0.071 / $0.085 / $0.141 per image**, 21 turns each, 123-700s, 15,045-27,841 tokens per image (dominated by cache reads -- the whole image context re-reads every turn). That is **1.6x to 4x the $0.0346/image the vision-baseline task measured**, for the same model on the same images: per-image cost is a property of the harness, not the model, and a single measurement of it is not a budget. Spread across four runs of the same task is 2.6x. Any 168-page estimate must carry that range.

**v1 confirmed at n=3, and it is the tightest number in the study.** A third independent Sonnet pass on v1 gives pairwise Spearman **0.704 / 0.669 / 0.675** on the mean-of-axes -- a spread of 0.035 -- for **mean +0.683, ICC(3,1) 0.711**, centred MAE 3.30, centred/constant 0.70. Judged overall: 0.696 / 0.636 / 0.703, ICC 0.693. So Sonnet's test-retest on v1 is genuinely reproducible, and the mean-of-axes edges out the judged overall on every statistic. Per-axis at n=3: **layout +0.636 (ICC 0.748), hierarchy +0.676 (0.626), density +0.586 (0.674)** all beat their constant controls; **typography +0.512 (0.418) and contrast +0.381 (0.296)** do not (ratios 1.30 and 1.49).

**The finding that kills per-axis reporting: which axes work is a property of the MODEL, not the rubric.** Same five axes, same anchors, same 18 pixels. Centred-error-over-constant (below 1.0 = the axis beats doing nothing): | axis | Sonnet (3 passes) | Opus (2 passes) | |---|---|---| | layout | **0.74** | 1.05 | | typography | 1.30 | 1.25 | | contrast | 1.49 | **0.60** | | density | **0.68** | **0.56** | | hierarchy | **0.70** | 1.16 | **Only `density` survives for both, and the two models' strong axes are otherwise opposite** -- contrast is Opus's best axis (ICC 0.728) and Sonnet's worst (ICC 0.296); layout and hierarchy are the reverse. Four of the five words are not pinning down a shared construct; each model has its own stable idiosyncratic reading. **Consequence: publish the headline mean, and show the per-axis prose as justification -- not the per-axis numbers.**

**v2's third pass FAILED, and the failure is evidence.** `API Error: Claude's response exceeded the 32000 output token maximum` after **1,506s and $3.93 spent for zero output**. v1 completed 3 of 3. The v2 rubric asks for numbered, region-naming prose across 6 axes x 18 images and that overflows the default output cap -- so beyond being 17x less reliable, v2 is also the arm that does not finish. v2 therefore rests on 2 passes, not 3; stated plainly rather than quietly. It does not change the verdict: Spearman +0.039 vs +0.683, with the mechanism identified from the prose and reproduced on two separate pages.

**The one change that IS supported, and it is free: average two passes.** Spearman-Brown on Sonnet's measured single-pass ICC of 0.711 -- reliability of a k-pass mean = k*ICC/(1+(k-1)*ICC): **k=1 -> 0.711 | k=2 -> 0.831 | k=3 -> 0.881 | k=4 -> 0.908 | k=5 -> 0.925.** Two passes averaged buys 0.83 for double the money and is the value-for-money point; the fourth and fifth passes buy almost nothing. This is the fix that the rubric REWRITE was supposed to deliver and did not: the noise is in the sampling, not the wording, so you beat it by sampling twice rather than by rewording.

**COST, measured over 7 real CLI runs (deliverable input).** claude-sonnet-5, 18 images per pass, this harness: successful v1 passes cost **$1.28 / $1.53 / $1.84 = $0.071 / $0.085 / $0.102 per image** (mean **$0.086**), 21-31 turns, 216-281s, and 15,045 / 23,709 / **72,278** tokens per image -- a **4.8x spread in tokens across three identical runs**, all cache-read dominated because the whole image context re-reads every turn. The vision-baseline task measured $0.0346/image for the same model on the same images with a different harness. **So per-image cost is a property of the harness and the turn count, not of the model, and it varies 3x run to run.** Total CLI spend for this task: **$12.66** across 7 runs (4 scoring passes at n=2/3, one 3rd-pass retry that failed at $3.93, two smoke tests).

**168 pages, costed, at the recommended two-passes-averaged setting.** Per page = 2 x per-image. At this harness's measured mean ($0.086/image): **$0.17/page, $28.90 for 168.** At the leaner vision-baseline harness ($0.0346/image): **$0.069/page, $11.63 for 168.** So **$12-$29 for the whole site, twice over** -- and the honest figure is a range, not a point, because three identical runs varied 3x. Screenshots are free (global Playwright, one context, ~2 min for 168 at 1280). Single-pass would halve it to $6-$15 and drop reliability from 0.83 to 0.71, which is not a trade worth making at these absolute numbers. **Cost is not the blocker on this program; the missing reference standard is.**

**DELIVERABLE 5 -- THE VERDICT. Not yet, and the blocker is a missing reference standard, not the rubric and not the model.** Run it over 168 pages **only as a self-consistent relative ranker**: `claude-sonnet-5`, the **v1** axes unchanged, **two passes averaged**, reporting **the mean of the five axes** and the per-axis prose but **not** the per-axis numbers, **no rescale**, at **$0.07-$0.17 per page ($12-$29 for the site)**. That configuration is defensible: measured test-retest ICC 0.711 single-pass and 0.83 for the 2-pass mean, tight across three runs (0.704 / 0.669 / 0.675). What it is NOT is validated against how pages actually look. **The designated source of truth reproduces itself at ICC 0.510 -- worse than the cheap tier it was built to grade -- and Sonnet agrees with it at only Spearman +0.12 to +0.26, while agreeing with itself at +0.68.** Two reliable scorers measuring different things is what that pattern means, and nothing in this program can adjudicate between them, because there is no third party. Three consequences follow: the vision-baseline verdicts that rest on single-draw coefficients (Sonnet's +0.625, 'taste beats math at ranking') do not replicate; per-axis scores are not publishable because which axes work flips between models; and my own fact-anchored rewrite made reliability 17x worse, so the wording is not the lever. **The one artifact that unblocks everything: a reference that is not one pass by one model -- Mike ordering the 18 frozen shots best-to-worst by eye (an afternoon, and it settles which of Opus, Sonnet, taste and math is measuring the right thing), or an averaged multi-pass panel adopted as the standard. Until that exists, ship the ranker, show the prose, and do not put a number in front of Mike as if it were true.**

**What I did NOT reach, plainly.** (a) v2's third pass failed on the output cap and was not retried -- v2 rests on 2 passes. (b) I did not build the corrected v3 (one criterion per anchor, holistic bands) or test it: designing a third rubric from a two-pass failure and validating it with two more passes is exactly the 'retune off one run' trap, so the correction is recorded in rubric.md as the next experiment, not shipped. (c) Haiku was not re-run on either rubric -- vision-baseline's verdict that it is a constant-70 generator stands unchallenged and I had no reason to spend against it. (d) No new pages were shot and no page was scored outside the frozen 18, per the fences. (e) `ext/LayoutTool/**` untouched; its four calibration bugs remain as vision-baseline logged them, and nothing here contradicts them -- but note that bug #1's evidence (taste's width-used dead band) is unaffected by any of this, since it is a code defect rather than a judgement.

assign.outcome: **NOT YET — and the blocker is a missing reference standard, not the rubric and not the model.** The baseline does not reproduce itself: a blind Opus re-score of the same 18 pixels against the same anchors gives **MAE 7.89 / Spearman +0.507 / ICC 0.510**, and on four of six axes it carries no more information than a fixed number. **Sonnet agrees with the baseline better than the baseline agrees with itself** (+0.625 vs pass A, +0.689 vs my pass B) and reproduces ITSELF at **ICC 0.711** across three passes — so the cheap tier is the more repeatable scorer and the designated source of truth is the least. **Rescale verified: the Spearman-cannot-move check PASSES exactly** (delta 0.000, ranks identical, no bug) — but reject it anyway: it raises MAE above a constant, no monotone map can reach the tail (Sonnet ties the corpus's worst page with three mid-pack pages, so flow stays ≥17.8 points high under any rescale), and its two parameters are the reference's own mean and sd. **`contrast` does do two jobs** — pass A's prose proves legibility and emphasis cancelling on the same page — but it is the *most* reproducible axis (ICC 0.728), so I built the split, **tested it, and rejected it**: a 4-pass controlled experiment (2 rubrics × identical harness/images) put my fact-anchored v2 at **ICC 0.041 against v1's 0.711**, because multi-criterion anchors with no combining rule turn a difference in attention into 55 points of score. **Ship: Sonnet, v1 axes unchanged, two passes averaged (ICC 0.83), headline mean only, no per-axis numbers, no rescale, $0.07–$0.17/page = $12–$29 for 168.** Deliverables: `rubric.md`, `agreement.json`, `pass-b.json`; `baseline.json` untouched and all 18 hashes verified. **The one artifact that unblocks the program: Mike ordering the 18 frozen shots best-to-worst by eye.**

log.msg: Files written by this task, all inside its own dir: `rubric.md` (the production hand-off — v1 axes, the two-pass protocol, the rejected rewrite, the open blocker), `agreement.json` (every number: Opus self-agreement, all tiers vs BOTH baselines, the rescale verification, the v1-vs-v2 experiment, Spearman-Brown), `pass-b.json` (the blind second Opus pass, so the repeatability number is reproducible), `task.jsonl`, `requirements.md`. **`../vision-baseline/baseline.json` was not modified** — verified read-only throughout, and all 18 PNG hashes re-checked as byte-identical before scoring. No site page, no `ext/**`, no `Server/**` touched. Machinery (the shoot-free harness, prompts, stats scripts) stayed in the session scratchpad per RULE#12.

**DELIVERABLE 2 completed as a conclusion in the repo, not just a claim.** `experiment.json` carries the raw per-page scores from all five completed passes (v1 x3, v2 x2) with each pass's cost, tokens, turns and wall time -- so the ICC 0.711 vs 0.041 comparison is recomputable from the repo without the scratchpad. The split axes' full 30/60/90 anchors are preserved verbatim in `rubric.md`, marked not-for-production, so the next attempt at the split starts from the tested wording and its known failure rather than reinventing it. Machinery (prompts, shoot-free harness, stats scripts) stayed in the scratchpad per RULE#12.

**A note that cuts against my own conclusions, in the spirit of 'instruments find themselves first'.** Every reliability figure here rests on n=18 images and 2-3 passes. ICC at n=18 has wide confidence intervals -- 0.711 and 0.510 are a real difference in point estimate but I have not established they differ significantly, and I did not compute intervals. What IS robust: v1's three pairwise Spearmans span 0.035 (0.704 / 0.669 / 0.675), so that number is stable; v2's collapse is large enough (0.039) that no plausible interval reaches v1; and the per-axis constant-control ratios are direction-consistent across both models on `density` and both fail on `typography`. What is NOT robust and should not be quoted as settled: the exact ordering of the middle axes, and any claim that Opus is significantly less reliable than Sonnet rather than merely measured lower. **Do not retune anything off this single study -- including the recommendation to use two passes, which is a projection from Spearman-Brown, not a measurement of a 2-pass panel.**
